analysis.one_liner: Exempts approved pesticide applications from Clean Water Act discharge permits.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 13 Senate sponsors split evenly between the parties, the bill died in the Environment and Public Works Committee without a hearing, a markup, or any vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After a 2009 federal court decision, pesticide sprays and residues applied in or near rivers, lakes, and streams generally need a Clean Water Act permit — a process that imposes monitoring, public notice, and water-quality conditions on the people doing the spraying. This bill would change federal law so that any pesticide approved for sale and use under the pesticide-control law (FIFRA) can be applied without a water permit, keeping only narrow exceptions for illegal applications, stormwater, and industrial or vessel discharges. Supporters argued FIFRA registration already protects water and the permit is a duplicate; the bill also directed EPA to report on whether FIFRA could be strengthened for water quality.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main gainers would be agricultural operations, aerial applicators, mosquito-control and weed-control programs, and pesticide manufacturers. They would be freed from applying for and complying with National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permits — paperwork, fees, monitoring, and conditions — whenever their sprays or residues reach navigable waters.

how_it_helps.text: Would prohibit EPA or any state from requiring a Clean Water Act permit for discharges into navigable waters of a pesticide authorized under FIFRA or its residues resulting from its application [S2][S3].
Keeps narrow exceptions: discharges from applications that violate FIFRA water-quality provisions, regulated stormwater, and industrial, treatment-works, and vessel-operation discharges [S2][S3].
Directs EPA, with the Agriculture Department, to report to congressional committees on how pesticide registration under FIFRA could better protect water quality and human health [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on people who drink, fish, swim in, or draw from the waters where pesticides are applied. Without permits, there is no site-specific limit, no monitoring requirement, no public notice, and no Clean Water Act enforcement backstop for what ends up in the water; the public bears the health and environmental risk and the cost of discovering problems after the fact.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the Clean Water Act's only case-by-case check on pesticide discharges. A FIFRA label is written for a specific use, not for the specific water body being sprayed, so it does not address how much pesticide a particular stream, reservoir, or fish population can absorb [S2][S3].
Without permits, there is no monitoring of pesticide levels in receiving waters and no public record of where and how much pesticide is entering lakes, rivers, and drinking-water sources [S2][S3].

Supporters' strongest objection, which an honest backer would acknowledge: the permit obligation — created after a 2009 court decision — does impose real costs on farmers, aerial applicators, and local mosquito-abatement programs, including for routine public-health spraying, and it overlaps with FIFRA's own water-quality review.

The bill's own 'report' provision concedes the point of the criticism: it asks EPA to study whether FIFRA, the sole remaining framework if the bill passed, needs modification to better protect water quality and human health — meaning the exemption would take effect before anyone knew whether FIFRA was adequate on its own [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Applicators and manufacturers would get a genuine, ongoing cost saving by ending a duplicate permitting process. The trade is that the public loses the one legal mechanism that sets water-specific limits, requires monitoring, and allows Clean Water Act enforcement for pesticide residues in shared waters. Because FIFRA registration does not evaluate each affected water body, and the bill's own directive to study FIFRA's adequacy would come after the exemption took effect, the cost side is real and hard to reverse. This is a straightforward deregulation whose benefits are concentrated and whose risks are spread across the public.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in late September 2012 with bipartisan sponsorship, it was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it; the bill expired when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

narrative.text: Hagan and nine original cosponsors — including six Republicans and three other Democrats — introduced the bill on September 20, 2012 [S1][S3].
It was read twice and referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works [S1][S5].

The full recorded action history contains only the introduction and the committee referral; no hearing, markup, committee vote, floor vote, or further action ever occurred before the Congress ended [S5].
Twelve senators later cosponsored the bill, six Republicans and six Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the existing Clean Water Act permit requirement for pesticide discharges stayed in place. People who drink from, fish in, and recreate in treated waters kept their monitoring, notice, and enforcement protections; pesticide users and manufacturers did not get the exemption they sought, though they also avoided nothing new since the bill changed nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Water users; permit rules stayed in place

for.name: Sen. Kay Hagan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought an exemption from Clean Water Act permitting for approved pesticide applications.

for.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, giving the bill Republican leadership in the Senate.

for.name: 12 cosponsoring senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; six Republicans and six Democrats signed on in the roughly three months it was alive.

against.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the committee during its three-plus months before the Congress expired.

against.name: Environmental and clean-water organizations
against.what_they_did: Opposed repealing the Clean Water Act permit requirement for pesticide discharges and pressed against similar House legislation.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was genuinely bipartisan — the 13 original introducers split 6 Republicans and 7 Democrats, and the eventual cosponsor list split 6 Republicans and 6 Democrats [S1][S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill would make FIFRA registration the only federal review of pesticide discharges to water, eliminating the permit layer that could add conditions or restrictions after registration. Their gain comes at the cost of the public's water-quality oversight.

industries.industry: Agricultural producers and aerial pesticide applicators
industries.note: They would be freed from Clean Water Act permit applications, fees, monitoring, and conditions whenever sprays or residues reach navigable waters. The savings come at the expense of monitoring and limits on what enters shared waters.

industries.industry: Mosquito-control and other public pesticide programs
industries.note: Public-health spraying programs are the permit holders whose paperwork burden the bill would remove. As government agencies they serve the public, but the exemption would also remove oversight of what they discharge.

industries.industry: Environmental monitoring, water utilities, and fisheries interests
industries.note: Without the permit trigger, less data would exist on pesticide levels in source waters, and water systems and fisheries would absorb whatever residues arrive with no Clean Water Act hook to limit them.
